_note: Separate from data/image_rules/rules_v1.json on purpose. That file records Amazon's published requirements and changes when Amazon changes them; this one records OUR detector's measured calibration and changes when we re-measure. Mixing them would mean a recalibration bumped the 'Amazon rules verified_on' date.
_calibrated_false_means: No threshold here has been measured against a labeled pair set. Until it has, find_near_duplicates() returns an empty report with calibrated=false and a reason, rather than inventing a cutoff. A detector reporting duplicates at an unmeasured threshold is reporting whatever its author felt like.

phash._what: DCT low-frequency block against its median. Robust to rescaling and recompression because those barely touch low frequencies.

dhash._what: Horizontal gradient signs on a 9x8 thumbnail. Cheap, sensitive to any global change.

tiles._what: A dHash per cell of a 4x4 grid; distance is the number of DISAGREEING cells. Robust to LOCALIZED edits - a badge pasted in one corner destroys one or two cells and leaves fourteen. Does NOT buy crop robustness: a crop shifts content across cell boundaries so cell i no longer corresponds to cell i.

_calibration_protocol._task_definition_correction: The build plan proposed 'same-product-different-shot' pairs as POSITIVES. That is wrong for this task and would have trained the threshold on the wrong question. Near-duplicate detection asks 'are these the SAME IMAGE?' - a second, genuinely different photo of the same product is not a duplicate, it is a legitimate additional image the seller should have. Same-product-different-shot therefore belongs in the NEGATIVES, and it is the HARD negative that makes the measurement meaningful. (The 'different shots of one product' question is a real task, but it is the benchmark half's image2image retrieval task, not dedup.)
_calibration_protocol.positives: Scripted mutations of one source image, with known expected outcomes: resize 75%/50%, JPEG q60/q30, corner badge, centre watermark, 5% border crop, brightness shift.
_calibration_protocol.hard_negatives: Different images of the SAME product (same ASIN). The discriminating case.
_calibration_protocol.reporting: Precision and recall reported against hard and easy negatives SEPARATELY. A method that only separates easy negatives is not useful - a listing's own images are all of one product.
_calibration_protocol.split: Threshold picked on a dev split of ASINs and reported on held-out ASINs. Split by ASIN, not by pair, so a product's images cannot appear on both sides.
metrics: precision and recall at the selected threshold
_calibration_protocol.pre_committed_outcome: Perceptual hashing was designed for exactly this task, so it may beat or tie a CLIP embedding. If it does, report it and ship hashing only - that saves hosting a model, and it is the same pre-commitment this repo makes for frozen CLIP versus the fine-tune.

featureless_guard._is_a_guard_not_a_calibrated_threshold: Unlike max_distance, this is not tuned against a labeled set - it exists to reject degenerate INPUT, not to decide a verdict. Every hash here encodes contrast structure, so an image with none produces a degenerate hash: measured, a flat white square and a flat grey square both hash to 0x0000000000000000 under dHash AND pHash, giving distance 0 between two visibly different images. Images below this std are excluded from dedup and reported as skipped, rather than being called duplicates of each other.

group_mismatch._why: A mismatch is only reported when the nearest out-of-group image is within the CALIBRATED duplicate threshold. Without that gate the check reported a mismatch whenever an image's nearest neighbour happened to sit in another group at any distance - measured on seven real product images, all pairwise dHash distances fell between 19 and 35 bits, so the nearest-group ordering was arbitrary and 5 of 7 images were flagged. Reusing the measured duplicate threshold makes the claim precise: 'this image is a near-duplicate of an image you tagged to a different SKU.'
